Elongated bristlemouth fish Sigmops elongatus is a mesopelagic species distributed widely across the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, where it occupies the dimly lit waters of the continental slope and open ocean. Females of this gonostomatid reach a maximum recorded body length of 27.5 centimeters [Li = 27.5 centimeters], a value derived from extensive trawl surveys conducted throughout its range. Reproductive maturity is attained at a markedly smaller size, with individuals typically becoming capable of spawning once they achieve a fork length of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters]. This disparity between maturation size and ultimate length suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth following the onset of reproductive activity, a life-history strategy observed in several other mesopelagic teleosts. The age at which puberty occurs has not been directly determined for this species, though growth-interval estimates from related gonostomatids indicate that the transition to maturity likely requires several years under the cold thermal regime of its deep-water habitat. Such a pattern of delayed maturation followed by extended growth may represent an adaptation to the low and unpredictable food availability characteristic of the mesopelagic zone.

Data on the wet weight at birth for Sigmops elongatus remain limited owing to the difficulty of collecting viable, fertilised ova from deep-water spawning grounds. However, based on the egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters observed in the closely related Maurolicus muelleri, the estimated wet weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams]. This minute body mass is typical of species that produce small, pelagic eggs with limited yolk reserves, a reproductive strategy that results in a weakly developed yolk-sac larva that relies on endogenous nutrients for only a brief period after eclosion. The transition to exogenous feeding must occur rapidly, as the energetic buffer provided by the residual yolk is insufficient to sustain prolonged starvation. Field observations of congeneric species suggest that the mouth-closed prolarva begins active prey capture within a few days of hatching, a critical window during which mortality from starvation is exceptionally high in the food-scarce mesopelagic environment.

As female Sigmops elongatus continue their somatic growth beyond the size at first maturation, they accumulate substantial body mass over the course of their adult life. The ultimate female wet weight attained by this species, calculated from the length-weight relationship derived for gonostomatid fishes, reaches approximately 66.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 66.2 grams]. In contrast, the wet weight at which females typically achieve puberty is estimated at 25.2 grams [Wwp = 25.2 grams], indicating that the reproductive lifespan spans a period during which body mass more than doubles. This substantial post-maturational growth trajectory is reflected in the positive allometric scaling observed between length and mass, with the exponent of 3.03 suggesting that larger females become disproportionately heavier relative to their increase in length. Such a pattern may confer fecundity advantages, as larger, older individuals are often capable of producing more oocytes per spawning event and may also contribute higher-quality yolk reserves to their developing offspring, thereby enhancing larval survival in the challenging pelagic environment.

At the prevailing water temperature of 6.9 °C [T = 6.9 °C] characteristic of the species' mesopelagic habitat, the daily reproductive output of a female Sigmops elongatus that has attained the pubertal length of 20 centimeters has been modelled from energetic principles. The estimated reproductive rate at this size corresponds to approximately 5000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 5000 eggs per year], a fairly modest annual fecundity for a mesopelagic teleost. This species produces roughly 14 eggs per reproductive event [N_R_i = roughly 14 eggs per reproductive event] and engages in approximately 350 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 350 spawning events per year]. The relatively low daily fecundity likely reflects the constraints imposed by the cold, low-productivity environment, where somatic growth and gamete production must be fuelled by a sparse and intermittent food supply. It is noteworthy that the reproductive rate is temperature-dependent, and the value cited here is specific to the thermal conditions of the deep scattering layer, where temperatures remain stable but low throughout the year.

The maximum recorded lifespan of Sigmops elongatus at the ambient temperature of 6.9 °C [T = 6.9 °C] found in its preferred depth range is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years], a relatively brief duration for a fish of its ultimate body size. This longevity estimate aligns closely with values reported for other small gonostomatids and reflects the accelerated metabolic pace imposed by the cold, food-limited mesopelagic environment.
